query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy multilayers, a modulation period (λ) of 16 nm creates semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces that induce localized dislocation pileups and high interfacial stress. This stress promotes interfacial amorphization, which in turn lowers atomic-migration barriers, thereby shifting the creep mechanism from dislocation-mediated slip/climb to atomic-diffusion- or interface-slip-mediated deformation. This change in mechanism explains the enhanced room-temperature creep resistance relative to multilayers with coherent (λ = 8 nm) or grain-boundary-dominated (λ = 32/80 nm) interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, approximately 1 μm-thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings produced from Al0.2CrFeNi and Al targets.
generation.intervention: Vary the modulation period (individual layer thickness, λ) during RF magnetron sputtering deposition to produce multilayers with λ = 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm, followed by room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing.
generation.conditions: Deposition under base pressure of ~5 × 10^-4 Pa, Ar flow of 100 sccm, working pressure of 0.3 Pa, with 150 W applied on the HEA target and alternating 0/30 W on the Al target over 1 h. Nanoindentation creep tests at room temperature with a 5 mN maximum load, loading rates of 1, 0.1, and 0.01 mN/s, a 100 s hold, and 20 s unloading; indentation depths approximately 1/10–1/7 of the coating thickness.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface coherency; specifically, the semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces in the 16 nm multilayer contain misfit dislocations that generate stress concentrations conducive to interfacial amorphization.
generation.mechanism: Semicoherent interfaces block dislocation glide, resulting in dislocation pileups and high localized interfacial stress. This promotes amorphization at the interface, increasing free volume and disorder that lower atomic-migration barriers, thus facilitating a diffusion- or interface-slip-mediated creep mechanism rather than traditional dislocation slip or climb.
generation.predicted_outcome: The 16 nm (M16) semicoherent multilayer will exhibit the highest room-temperature creep resistance reflected by a lower creep strain rate and a creep stress exponent (n) indicative of diffusion/interface-slip mechanisms (n around 1–2), in contrast to 8 nm (coherent interfaces) and 32/80 nm (grain-boundary-dominated) samples, which will show higher creep rates and stress exponents (n > 3) characteristic of dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.baseline: The comparison baseline is the multilayers with coherent interfaces (λ = 8 nm, M8) and those dominated by grain boundaries (λ = 32 and 80 nm, M32/M80), which are expected to deform primarily by dislocation slip or climb.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to ~1 μm thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni sputtered multilayers tested at room temperature under nanoindentation creep conditions (5 mN load, loading rates of 1–0.01 mN/s). Its applicability outside these conditions, such as at elevated temperatures or with macroscopic creep tests, remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While prior MD/HRTEM work provides some support for stress-induced amorphization at semicoherent interfaces, directly linking this amorphization to the observed creep resistance requires further experimental confirmation. The precise correlation between interfacial structure and creep stress exponent also has inherent uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multilayer coatings with controlled modulation periods (8, 16, 32, 80 nm) under the same deposition conditions. Characterize the interface structure using XRD and TEM/IFFT to confirm the nature (coherent, semicoherent, or grain-boundary dominated) of the interfaces. Perform room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing at multiple loading rates to extract the creep strain rate and deduce the creep stress exponent (n).
measurements: XRD and TEM/IFFT to characterize interface coherency and detect amorphization
Load–displacement and displacement–dwell-time nanoindentation curves to determine creep behavior
Linear fits of ln(strain rate) versus ln(flow stress) to determine the creep stress exponent, distinguishing diffusion/interface-slip (n ~1–2) from dislocation-mediated creep (n >3)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 16 nm multilayer does not show a significantly higher creep resistance and a transition to a lower creep stress exponent (n closer to 1–2) relative to both the 8 nm and 32/80 nm multilayers, then the proposed mechanism involving stress-induced interfacial amorphization as the rate-limiting factor for creep is falsified.
